body_html:
Grocery shopping in Spanish is one of the best everyday practice sessions you can get. Whether you are in a big supermarket in Monterrey, a neighborhood market in Mexico City, a Latino grocery store in Houston or a market in Madrid, the conversations are short and predictable: asking where something is, ordering at the counter, checking prices and paying. Learn the phrases below and you can handle all of them.

Quick answer
  • Asking: Disculpe, ¿dónde está la leche?
  • At the counter: Me da medio kilo de jamón, por favor.
  • Prices: ¿Cuánto cuesta? ¿A cómo está el aguacate?
  • Checkout: ¿Aceptan tarjeta? No necesito bolsa, gracias.
{{toc}}

Grocery shopping in Spanish: finding things

SpanishEnglish
Disculpe, ¿dónde está el arroz?Excuse me, where is the rice?
¿Dónde encuentro los huevos?Where can I find the eggs?
¿Tienen tortillas de harina?Do you have flour tortillas?
¿En qué pasillo está?Which aisle is it in?
Ya no hay.There’s none left.
Se acabó.It’s sold out.

Store workers will often answer with directions like al fondo (at the back), a la derecha (on the right) or en el pasillo cinco (in aisle five). For more on directions, see {{link:asking-for-directions-in-spanish|asking for directions in Spanish}}.

At the deli, meat and produce counters

At a counter, you order the same way you would in a restaurant, with a polite question:

  • Me da medio kilo de queso Oaxaca, por favor. Could I have half a kilo of Oaxaca cheese, please?
  • ¿Me lo puede rebanar delgadito? Could you slice it thin for me?
  • Un kilo de tomates, por favor. A kilo of tomatoes, please. (In Mexico, red tomatoes are jitomates.)
  • ¿Están maduros los aguacates? Are the avocados ripe?
  • Es todo, gracias. That’s all, thanks.

Latin America and Spain use the metric system: un kilo is about 2.2 pounds and medio kilo about 1.1 pounds. Cien gramos is a small amount, about a quarter of a pound. In Spain, you will hear ¿Me pone…? at the counter.

{{image:2}}

Talking about prices

SpanishEnglish
¿Cuánto cuesta?How much does it cost?
¿Cuánto es?How much is it? (the total)
¿A cómo está el kilo?How much per kilo?
¿Está en oferta?Is it on sale?
Está muy caro.It’s very expensive.
¿Me hace un descuentito?Could you give me a little discount? (markets only)

Bargaining is normal at open-air markets like the Mexican tianguis, but not in supermarkets. The diminutive descuentito softens the request and usually earns a smile.

At the checkout

  • ¿Aceptan tarjeta? Do you take cards?
  • Pago en efectivo. I’ll pay cash.
  • No necesito bolsa, gracias. Traje la mía. I don’t need a bag, thanks. I brought my own.
  • ¿Me da el ticket, por favor? Could I have the receipt, please?
  • ¿Quiere redondear? Would you like to round up? (a common donation request in Mexico)

In Mexico, supermarket baggers are often older adults or students who work for tips, so having a few coins ready is appreciated.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

A sample conversation at the market

Vendedor: ¡Pásele, güera! ¿Qué le damos?
Come on in! What can I get you?

Tú: Buenos días. ¿A cómo están los aguacates?
Good morning. How much are the avocados?

Vendedor: A sesenta el kilo. Están bien buenos.
Sixty pesos a kilo. They’re really good.

Tú: Deme un kilo, por favor. ¿Están para hoy?
Give me a kilo, please. Are they ready to eat today?

Vendedor: Sí, estos ya están listos. ¿Algo más?
Yes, these are ready. Anything else?

Tú: Es todo, gracias.
That’s all, thanks.

¡Pásele! is the classic Mexican market welcome, and vendors often use friendly nicknames like güera or joven for customers. Asking whether fruit is para hoy (for today) or para mañana is a smart market habit.

Shopping lists: words you will need

Here are the basics for a weekly list: leche (milk), huevos (eggs), pan (bread), arroz (rice), frijoles (beans), pollo (chicken), carne molida (ground beef), queso (cheese), cebolla (onion), ajo (garlic), limones (limes, in Mexico), café and papel de baño (toilet paper). Writing your list in Spanish is an easy daily habit that builds vocabulary without any extra study.

{{image:3}}

Food words that change by country

Grocery vocabulary varies more than almost any other area. A few examples:

EnglishMexicoSpain
tomatojitomatetomate
avocadoaguacateaguacate (palta in Argentina and Chile)
beansfrijolesjudías, alubias
peachduraznomelocotón
strawberryfresafresa (frutilla in Argentina)
chili pepperchileguindilla

I explore more of these differences in {{link:latin-american-vs-spain-spanish|Latin American vs Spain Spanish}}.

Common mistakes

  • Quiero un kilo de tomates. Not wrong, but blunt. ¿Me da un kilo de jitomates? sounds friendlier. See {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.
  • ¿Cuánto cuesta esto? while pointing at many items. For the total, ask ¿Cuánto es? or ¿Cuánto le debo?
  • Una bolsa plástica de papel. Plastic is bolsa de plástico; paper is bolsa de papel.
  • Using pounds. Outside the US, think in kilos and grams.

The RAE dictionary marks regional food words like jitomate and durazno with the countries where they are used.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Grocery shopping in Spanish is low pressure, repeats every week and rewards a few polite phrases. Start with ¿dónde está…?, ¿me da…? and ¿cuánto es?, learn the words for the foods you actually buy, and soon the market will be one of your favorite places to practice. For other everyday moments, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you ask where something is in a Spanish supermarket?
faq.a: Disculpe, ¿dónde está…? or ¿Dónde encuentro…?, followed by the product.

faq.q: How do you order at the deli counter in Spanish?
faq.a: Use ¿Me da…? with the amount: ¿Me da medio kilo de jamón, por favor? In Spain, ¿Me pone…? is also common.

faq.q: Is it okay to bargain when grocery shopping in Spanish-speaking countries?
faq.a: At open-air markets, a friendly request for a discount is normal. In supermarkets, prices are fixed.
A traditional open-air street market in Mexico, usually held on a set day each week.
